item.title: Nationwide ground stop over: Guam, CNMI flights were not affected
item.description: UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration announced the groundstop was lifted and domestic air travel was able to resume. Earlier Saturday, airport officials on Guam and in the CNMI said the nationwide grounding of domestic air traffic did not affect local airports here.
item.content:encoded:
UPDATE: The Federal Aviation Administration announced the groundstop was lifted and domestic air travel was able to resume.

Earlier Saturday, airport officials on Guam and in the CNMI said the nationwide grounding of domestic air traffic did not affect local airports here.

An announcement from the Guam International Airport Saturday said officials are “closely monitoring the situation. No Guam flights are affected as of yet, and operations remain normal.”

Travelers were advised to keep in touch with their air carriers through official mobile apps to get the latest flight information.

The airport said the situation is still developing, and “GIAA will continue to closely monitor it and share information as circumstances change.”

The Commonwealth Ports Authority said inter-island flights between Saipan, Tinian and Rota were operating normally.

While Saturday morning’s Guam flight arrived and departed from Saipan, the agency said other flights outside of the CNMI may still be delayed or canceled.

Star Marianas Air posted a social media status update Saturday saying the company’s flights were not affected by the FAA nationwide stop.

Update from The White House https://t.co/pNjkz3znSB

Early Saturday, Guam time, NPR reported that the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a "communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers," according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy.

The FAA said the ground stop was linked to a "temporary telecommunications outage."

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin told reporters at the White House there was no indication that the problem stemmed from a threat to the United States, NPR reported.

item.content:encoded:
The Department of Public Health and Social Services is reminding families who received 2026 Summer Electronic Benefit Transfer benefits to use any remaining funds by Nov. 16.

The federally funded program helps eligible families purchase food for school-aged children during the summer months. Under federal requirements, any unused benefits will be returned to the funding source after the expiration date.

Families are encouraged to check their card balances and use their remaining benefits before Nov. 16. However, those who received their child’s card later and were given a different expiration date should follow the date provided.

Families who have not picked up their child’s Summer EBT card or need a replacement may visit the Bureau of Economic Security office on the second floor of the RanCare Building in Tamuning from 8 a.m. to 4:30 p.m.Monday through Friday.

For assistance, families may contact the Summer EBT Call Center at (671)735-7325 or (671)735-7310, or email kidssebtguam@dphss.guam.gov .

Public Health administers the Summer EBT Program locally in partnership with the Guam Department of Education.

item.title: Hybrid Land Use Commission approves school in Tumon, extension for Tamuning subdivision
item.description: The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning. The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Hybrid Land Use Commission on Thursday approved using a vacant mall in Tumon as a school and granted a one-year extension for the construction of a subdivision in Tamuning.

The zone variance allows the unused Tumon Bay Mall, owned by Grandview Development, to be converted to a facility that will house 40 classrooms and up to 1,080 students from iLearn Academy, a charter school.

Architect Michael Blas Makio, managing principal at Taniguchi Ruth Makio Architects, said the project would be good for Tumon and good for education.

“Even driving here, we started the really sad exercise of counting the vacant buildings that we're seeing around the island, and that's a really scary growing number, right? So we’ve got to find these viable uses that we can bring into the space,” Makio said.

The vacant mall is located next to Garden Villa Hotel and across from Crowne Plaza Resort.

The Commission also granted a one-year extension for the construction of Oka Villas subdivision, located near Oka Pay-Less and Rosie’s Apartments in Tamuning.

The land has been cleared and utilities are being installed.

The subdivision will have 36 single-family residential lots, a playground and a percolation basin.

item.title: 'We can't let them down' -- After midterm wins, Democrats turn to charting path ahead

item.content:encoded:
DENVER — Democrats descended on Denver for a two-day conference that was half victory party, half sober look at the road ahead on delivering for the voters who elected them.

The "What's Next" conference, hosted by the group Majority Democrats, was scheduled long before Democrats outperformed expectations with their best electoral performance since Watergate. It brought together rising stars — like incoming Gov. Rob Sand in Iowa and Sen.-elect James Talarico in Texas — along with strategists, organizers, state and federal lawmakers and potential presidential contenders.

Held at a concert hall, with colorful artwork of party heavy hitters dotting the venue, Democrats attended sessions like "What Voters Want" and "What Needs To Change." The overwhelming emphasis from speakers was that Democrats have to earn back trust.

"We won races in places where we haven't won in a long time, even in some places where we've never won. And the message shouldn't be that [voters] are fully embracing the Democratic Party," said Colorado Rep. Jason Crow in an interview.

"It took us decades to dig ourselves in a hole and to push people away from us, and it's going to take us more than one cycle to earn that trust," said Crow, who is one of the party's recruitment co-chairs.

Anderson Clayton, chair of the North Carolina Democratic Party, took the party to task for not investing more in the South and in Black voters.

"When we say that Black voters are the base of our party, then I ask why are we not investing in a region of the country that on Tuesday night just proved everybody wrong of what is possible," said Clayton to much applause. "Rural America deserves the investment from the Democratic Party and we must run towards communities that our party has run away from."

Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg said Democrats shouldn't rest on their laurels.

"I think we are adequately politically traumatized by the last few cycles, so that we will not draw the wrong lessons from all of this," Buttigieg said. "Because here's the thing: it is yet to be written whether what we just experienced is one more oscillation from one side to the other and back, or whether it is the beginning of a tectonic movement changing American politics."

He said Democrats can learn from the current White House on two fronts, by having: "a bias towards action and a readiness to get things done coming out of the gate and at the very same time a readiness to plan for the long-term," adding Democrats should come out of the gate strong, with a rapid-fire series of bills to lower the cost of living.

Presumptive next Speaker of the House Hakeem Jeffries told the audience he has plans to do just that, with a robust agenda that includes reversing Medicaid cuts, banning congressional stock trading and mid-decade redistricting, establishing a statutory right to abortion, and overturning the Supreme Court's Citizens United decision that did away with limits on political spending by corporations and unions.

The conference itself was peppered with potential presidential contenders, including Buttigieg, New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, and California Rep. Ro Khanna, one of the few progressive speakers.

No one announced an official run, but many gave previews of their theory of the case.

"I do think it's important that whoever we hire to be the chief executive of this country knows how to run something, knows how to get stuff done, knows how to not just have a vision but knows how to deliver on it," Shapiro told reporters.

Someone who was previously kicking the tires for a possible White House bid — Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen — told reporters he's no longer considering it, as he instead pursues the top leadership post in the Senate .

Throughout the conference, Democrats debated whether and how to work with the Trump administration in order to deliver meaningful change for voters.

"If slapping Trump's name on it and putting it in gold letters would get it through — hell yes, I would do that," said Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin.

"The American people cannot wait two years for change, so we must work with President Trump," Talarico said. "We should make the final two years of his presidency the most productive of any American presidency."

But New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill added a note of caution, describing the president as a bad faith actor.

"The art of the deal to Trump is he figures out what you want, he leverages the you know what out of you, and keeps taking, taking, taking, and never delivers," Sherrill said. "My advice to Sen. Talarico is if Trump wants to work with us, we will lay out the agenda, and he can sign it."

item.title: FAA blames Friday's ground stop on 'equipment issue' during telecoms network upgrade
item.description: Updated November 15, 2026 at 5:47 AM ChST WASHINGTON— Friday's nationwide ground stop started when a contractor updated old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication lines, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 15, 2026 at 5:47 AM ChST

WASHINGTON— Friday's nationwide ground stop started when a contractor updated old Federal Aviation Administration telecommunication lines, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Saturday.

Tens of thousands of passengers across the U.S. are still stranded Saturday after the rare ground stop. Bryan Bedford, the FAA administrator who joined Duffy at Saturday's media briefing, said schedule problems should be resolved by Sunday evening.

Nearly 25,000 flights were delayed, and over 9,000 were cancelled on Friday, according to FlightAware , a flight tracking site. The disruption seeped into Saturday morning with more than 4,000 cancellations recorded, which is 18% of flights departing the U.S., according to data from Cirium, an aviation analytics company.

L3Harris, a long time contractor for the FAA, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location changing copper wire to fiber optics, Duffy said. "When I tell you that we're using old equipment, we're using old equipment," he said.

He said the FAA is still investigating the exact error that started flooding other routers in the air traffic control system, and if L3Harris was at all responsible.

"It's pretty straightforward work that we were doing yesterday at, again, a very remote location. So what we're working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning was it user error, installator error from L3Harris, or did they install a faulty router?"

In a statement on their website , L3Harris said they have been working with the FAA to modernize communication infrastructure, including converting copper wires to a fiber optic system. The contractor said they have completed more than 70% of those conversions.

"We are supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the Nov. 13 ground stop of our nation's air travel," the statement said. "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

These updates have been happening in American institutions for decades, Duffy said.

"Virtually every single institution in America has gone from copper to fiber, from analog to digital," Duffy said. "Just maybe the FAA is the last one to be doing this work because the investments haven't been made, but this is not complicated."

Bedford said there was no evidence of anything nefarious happening or any AI-related issues.

Since his time in office, Duffy said he's been asking Congress for money to make more upgrades. In July 2025, Congress approved $12.5 billion to modernize the nation's aging air traffic control system.

On Saturday, Duffy said again that the FAA needed more money for improvements.

"This is the moment, if we don't start to switch out our systems, when, how long are we going to wait, America, and Congress?" Duffy asked.

For about four hours on Friday, thousands of flights at U.S. airports were grounded in one of the biggest disruptions of the nation's air travel system since the terrorist attacks on September 11, 2001.

The aviation system is back online and slowly returning to normal Saturday morning, but delays and cancellations will continue, Duffy said. Bedford said all passengers will be put on new flights or they'll get a full refund, but that people should reach out to their airlines directly.

Flight boards at airports across the country Saturday morning continued to be riddled with red cancelled marks. At Tampa International Airport in Florida, people in the main terminal area before security curled up in chairs to grab a wink of sleep.

On Friday night, a flight board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in D.C. showed dozens of flights delayed into the early morning hours or cancelled.

Passengers Erin and Jake Britt spent half the day at the airport in D.C. on Friday. Their plane to Fort Lauderdale, Fla. boarded at 3 p.m. By 5:30 p.m., they were getting off the plane — but they were still in D.C.

"Overall, our plane was definitely annoyed, but reasonable," Erin Britt said, as the couple left the airport at 8 p.m. "People being upset and asking like, 'Well, how are you not prepared for this?' And it was like, 'Well, no one was prepared.'"

She said neither the pilot nor flight attendants had any more information than passengers."They seem just as in the dark," she said.

The pair decided to cancel their weekend trip, but the night didn't end there. They spent over nine hours overnight waiting on the JetBlue customer service call line to be reimbursed. "I was setting alarms in 20 minute intervals in case I fell asleep," Erin Britt said.

For people who had events or plans over the weekend – the delay added an extra layer of stress. Joe Romano and Maddie Cabana had a cruise leaving Orlando, Fla. Saturday afternoon.

"It was a big eye roll. I mean, I travel a lot for work already, so I'm constantly dealing with flight delays," Romano said. "When this happened, I was just like, 'Of course, it always happens to me.'"

"Just rather inconvenient and frustrating," Cabana added, as the pair contemplated checking their bags or going home. They even thought about driving to Florida. "Hopefully, everything will be fine. It'll all work out. It always does."

And it did— eventually. After their JetBlue flight was ultimately cancelled, they quickly booked another one on Southwest Airlines and made it early Saturday morning.

Others, like Suze DiPietro decided flying wasn't worth it anymore. Her husband drove about four hours down from Ocean City, New Jersey to pick her up in D.C. Luckily, they had friends in the area where they spent the night.

"My husband, my hero, is driving down from New Jersey to come get me," DiPietro said.

Other alternatives included people switching to Amtrak trains as they struggled to get to their destination. Although, even Amtrak's system had a brief outage Friday night.

item.title: Fuel crisis and protests pressure Chile's far-right president
item.description: Updated November 15, 2026 at 2:11 AM ChST SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.
item.content:encoded:
Updated November 15, 2026 at 2:11 AM ChST

SANTIAGO, Chile — Chile's ultraconservative president finds himself on the back foot after just eight months in power.

José Antonio Kast, a politician who spent a career railing against progressive issues, reproductive rights and welfare policies from the extreme fringes of right-wing politics, now finds himself with just 24% approval in the polls.

It is less than a year since Kast stormed to the presidency in December 2025 by avoiding all mention of his hardline stances on social matters, focusing instead on two hot-button issues whipped up in the national media: illegal immigration and public security.

But rather than pressing ahead with those at the top of his agenda, he has floundered. And as elsewhere around the Americas and worldwide, rising costs of living have come to hit him hard.

"Our salaries are maybe 20% of a European income, but with a similar cost of living – it's terrible," said Simón Echavarría, a 30-year-old architect, at a march in Santiago on Friday evening.

"We want to protest against the measures that have set us back on environmental issues, on human rights, even reducing the sentences of pedophiles – they are implementing things that nobody asked for," he said.

Behind him, heavily armed police blocked the streets and fired water cannons at protesters chanting and waving flags in the square.

Much of the recent ire stems from the revelation last month that Kast's government had signed decrees to cut the sentences of 56 prisoners whose crimes range from the rape of children to dictatorship-era human rights violations.

Kast has since admitted that this was an "error", but came out in support of the undersecretary who signed the decrees nonetheless.

But beneath the more egregious moves Kast has made in his first year in power is simmering discontent over affordability.

In July, Kast's government chose not to apply an anti-inflation tool available to the Chilean state to ease the rise in fuel prices brought about by the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran.

Protests exploded as prices shot up overnight and motorists joined long queues at gas stations to fill their tanks before the rise came into effect.

This week, Chile's formidable truckers' unions blockaded two major highways in an effort to exert pressure on the government and address high fuel prices.

On Friday, the strike was broken after the government backed down, sending a bill to Chile's congress which will reverse planned fuel price rises.

It is expected to be approved this month, but public anger continues to grow over the cost of living.

Politicians across the Americas who have enthusiastically aligned themselves with President Donald Trump are facing challenges similar to those confronting the U.S. administration, as rising fuel prices and the cost of everyday goods fuel public discontent.

In Argentina, far-right libertarian Javier Milei faces reelection in less than a year, with 60% of the country disapproving of his leadership amid spiraling inflation. In Peru, President Keiko Fujimori is also facing growing discontent, with 53% disapproving of her government, according to a recent Ipsos poll.

At the march in Santiago on Friday, 30-year-old veterinarian Patricia Pereira said that she was concerned about cuts to science funding, but that her discontent ran deeper.

"Here in Chile, it was a hard-won victory for children to have free education, achieved through protests, and now even that's also being called into question," she said.

Protests are likely to grow in Santiago if the government fails to address the rising cost of living. President Kast has shown little sign of doing so.

To the contrary, his budget proposal is making its way through Congress, with the government seeking cuts to education, culture, science and a host of social programs.
